metadata.title: Understanding teaching professionals' digital competence: What do PIAAC and TALIS reveal about technology-related skills, attitudes, and knowledge?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study pools teaching professionals from 11 European countries using microdata from PIAAC (adult PS-in-TRE) and TALIS (teacher questionnaire). For all computed statistics (distributions, cross-tabulations/correlations, and regression models), the authors state that survey weights were applied to account for the complex sampling designs of PIAAC and TALIS. In TALIS regression models, they also account for school-level clustering using survey procedures that produce correct standard errors. The manuscript does not report the specific weight variable names (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or any replicate-weight scheme, so the exact weight identifiers cannot be extracted, but the use of complex-survey weighting is explicit.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses pooled data from 11 European countries that participated in both PIAAC Cycle 1 Round 1 (2011–2012) and TALIS 2018. For PIAAC, the sample is restricted to respondents working in the education industry (ISIC/ISCO-based industry/occupation definitions), yielding 2,590 teaching professionals for the PS-in-TRE plausible-value analyses; respondents who did not take the PS-in-TRE test (n=164) were merged into the weak-skills group (Level 1 or below). For TALIS, the sample is restricted to teachers in lower/primary/upper secondary contexts as covered by TALIS, yielding 50,800 respondents for the attitude and knowledge item analyses. The study does not report additional task-level exclusions beyond the PS-in-TRE test non-participation handling and the stated item selection for attitudes/knowledge.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC Cycle 1 Round 1 (2011–2012) PS-in-TRE (adult problem solving in technology-rich environments)
main_findings.target_variable: PS-in-TRE skills proficiency (strong Level 3 vs weak Level 1 or below)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted logistic regression (country effects controlled, fixed categorical country effect). Weak-skills model: Nagelkerke R-squared = 0.13; Strong-skills model: Nagelkerke R-squared = 0.04. Reported effects include: Age (OR=1.57 for weak; OR=0.67 for strong), Language background non-native (OR=0.45 for weak; no significant effect for strong), Books at home (OR=0.80 for weak; no effect for strong), ICT use at work (OR=0.61 for weak; no effect for strong), ICT use outside work (OR=1.40 for weak; no effect for strong).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC Cycle 1 Round 1 PS-in-TRE the study leveraged Age group, Language background (native vs non-native), Highest formal education level, Number of books at home, and ICT use regularity at work to model PS-in-TRE skills proficiency, finding that higher age increased the probability of weak skills and decreased the probability of strong skills, while ICT use at work was associated with lower odds of weak skills but did not guarantee strong proficiency. This indicates that digital-skills support should be targeted especially toward older teaching professionals and those with weaker socio-educational resources, while also recognizing that workplace ICT use alone may not translate into high-level problem-solving competence.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC Cycle 1 Round 1 (2011–2012) PIAAC background item (self-assessed possession of computer skills needed at work)
main_findings.target_variable: Belief of possessing computer skills needed at work (attitude indicator)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted logistic regression (country effects controlled). Nagelkerke R-squared = 0.06. Significant predictors reported in Table 4: Age (OR=0.74), Gender (male) OR=2.30, ICT use outside work OR=1.40. (Other predictors were not retained as significant in the final model.)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC Cycle 1 Round 1 the study leveraged Age group, Gender, and ICT use regularity outside work to predict the belief that respondents possess the computer skills needed at work, finding that the probability was highest among the youngest respondents, males, and the most active ICT users outside work. This indicates that self-efficacy/attitude toward job-relevant digital skills is strongly patterned by age and gender and may be reinforced by out-of-work technology engagement, suggesting that professional development should address both skill-building and confidence for less active groups.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire (lower secondary focus; selected attitude items)
main_findings.target_variable: Attitude: ability to support student learning through ICT (linear regression outcome)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted linear regression (country effects controlled). Sample sizes: n=48,189; R-squared = 0.02. Significant predictors in Table 5: Subject category (Technology teacher b=0.38, beta=0.04), Physical education b=-0.38 (beta=-0.08), Mathematics/science b=0.04 (beta=0.02), Languages b=0.11 (beta=0.03). Age and gender were not consistently significant across all attitude outcomes (age not significant here; gender not significant for this outcome).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire the study leveraged Age group, Gender, Primary subject taught, and TALIS formal education level to predict teachers’ attitude toward supporting student learning through ICT, finding that subject category showed the clearest associations (technology teachers reported higher support and physical education teachers lower support), while age and gender were not consistently associated once other factors were controlled. This indicates that curriculum/subject specialization is a key lever for designing ICT integration support, rather than relying on demographic targeting alone.

main_findings.target_variable: Attitude: how often teachers let students use ICT in class (linear regression outcome)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted linear regression (country effects controlled). Sample sizes: n=38,042; R-squared = 0.03. Significant predictors in Table 5: Age (b=0.02, beta=0.04), Gender (male) b=-0.08 (beta=-0.05), Subject category: Class teachers b=-0.23 (beta=-0.13), Mathematics/science b=-0.25 (beta=-0.11), Languages b=-0.17 (beta=-0.05), Technology b=0.78 (beta=0.09), Physical education b=-0.71 (beta=-0.14).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire the study leveraged Age group, Gender, Primary subject taught, and TALIS formal education level to predict how often teachers let students use ICT in class, finding that subject category dominated the pattern (technology teachers reported the highest frequency, while physical education teachers reported the lowest), with additional small gender differences. This indicates that improving classroom ICT use may require subject-specific pedagogical guidance and support for teachers in low-ICT subject areas, alongside addressing gendered differences in perceived or enacted ICT practices.

main_findings.target_variable: Attitude: importance of investing in ICT in education (linear regression outcome)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted linear regression (country effects controlled). Sample sizes: n=47,570; R-squared = 0.02. Significant predictors in Table 5: Subject category Technology b=0.38 (beta=0.04), Physical education b=-0.38 (beta=-0.08), Mathematics/science b=-0.05 (beta=-0.03), Languages b=-0.07 (beta=-0.02). Formal education showed small effects (ISCED 5 or below b=0.06 beta=0.02; ISCED 6 b=0.05 beta=0.03), while age and gender were not consistently significant for this outcome.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire the study leveraged Age group, Gender, Primary subject taught, and TALIS formal education level to predict teachers’ valuation of investing in ICT, finding that technology teachers rated ICT investment as more important and physical education teachers as less important, with only small differences by formal education and limited demographic effects. This indicates that attitudes toward ICT investment are closely tied to teachers’ subject roles, implying that policy communication and professional development should be tailored to subject communities to build shared buy-in.

main_findings.target_variable: Knowledge: ICT included in formal education or training (logistic regression outcome)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted logistic regression (country effects controlled). Sample sizes: n=48,970; Nagelkerke R-squared = 0.13. Significant predictors in Table 6: Age OR=0.53 (b=-0.64), Gender (male) OR=1.36 (b=0.30), Subject category: Class teachers OR=0.84 (b=-0.18), Reading/writing/literature OR=0.64 (b=-0.44), Mathematics/science OR=1.25 (b=0.22), Social studies/history/religion OR=0.72 (b=-0.32), Languages OR=0.67 (b=-0.41), Technology OR=1.48 (b=0.40), Physical education OR=0.48 (b=-0.73).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire the study leveraged Age group, Gender, Primary subject taught, and TALIS formal education level to predict whether ICT was included in teachers’ formal education or training, finding that younger teachers were more likely to report ICT inclusion and that subject category strongly differentiated responses (technology teachers highest; physical education lowest). This indicates that pre-service and in-service ICT preparation is uneven across subject specializations and cohorts, supporting policy efforts to update teacher education curricula and ensure equitable ICT knowledge foundations.

main_findings.target_variable: Knowledge: feeling prepared for using ICT in teaching (linear regression outcome)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted linear regression (country effects controlled). Sample sizes: n=46,970; R-squared = 0.11. Significant predictors in Table 6: Age b=-0.23 (OR=0.53 reported in logistic form elsewhere; here b=-0.23 with OR column present), Gender (male) b=0.20 (beta=0.09), Subject category: Class teachers b=-0.24 (beta=-0.13), Reading/writing/literature b=-0.18 (beta=-0.06), Mathematics/science b=0.22 (beta=0.02), Social studies/history/religion b=-0.14 (beta=-0.04), Languages b=-0.14 (beta=-0.03), Technology b=0.52 (beta=0.05), Physical education b=-0.27 (beta=-0.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire the study leveraged Age group, Gender, Primary subject taught, and TALIS formal education level to predict teachers’ self-reported preparedness for using ICT in teaching, finding that preparedness declines with age and varies substantially by subject category (technology teachers higher; class teachers and physical education teachers lower). This indicates that professional development should prioritize older teachers and subject groups with lower preparedness, while also leveraging technology teachers as exemplars for peer learning.

main_findings.target_variable: Knowledge: need for professional development in ICT skills (linear regression outcome)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted linear regression (country effects controlled). Sample sizes: n=48,453; R-squared = 0.03. Significant predictors in Table 6: Age b=0.09 (beta=0.12), Gender (male) b=-0.12 (beta=-0.06), Subject category: Class teachers b=0.24 (beta=0.13), Reading/writing/literature b=0.12 (beta=0.04), Mathematics/science b=0.08 (beta=0.02), Social studies/history/religion b=0.08 (beta=0.02), Languages b=0.09 (beta=0.02), Technology b=-0.45 (beta=-0.05), Physical education b=0.14 (beta=0.03).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire the study leveraged Age group, Gender, and Primary subject taught to predict teachers’ need for professional development in ICT skills, finding that older teachers report greater need and that technology teachers report the least need, while physical education and class teachers report higher need. This indicates that ICT professional development should be differentiated by both cohort and subject specialization, with targeted upskilling for groups expressing the highest training needs.

main_findings.target_variable: Knowledge: participation in ICT-related professional development activities (logistic regression outcome)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted logistic regression (country effects controlled). Sample sizes: n=46,804; Nagelkerke R-squared = 0.01. Significant predictors in Table 6: Gender (male) OR=1.20 (b=0.19), Subject category: Class teachers OR=1.26 (b=0.23), Reading/writing/literature OR=1.21 (b=0.19), Technology OR=1.48 (b=0.40), Physical education OR=0.65 (b=-0.43). Age and other subject categories were not consistently significant in the final model.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire the study leveraged Age group, Gender, and Primary subject taught to predict participation in ICT-related professional development, finding that overall explanatory power was very low (Nagelkerke R-squared = 0.01) and that participation differences were limited, with some subject and gender effects. This indicates that simply offering ICT professional development may not ensure uptake, and policy should address barriers to participation (e.g., time, relevance, and support) rather than assuming that training demand automatically translates into attendance.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses PIAAC Cycle 1 Round 1 (2011–2012) PS-in-TRE plausible values and TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire items to examine digital competence components—measured skills, self-reported attitudes, and self-reported knowledge—among teaching professionals pooled across 11 European countries. The authors apply survey-weighted descriptive statistics and regression models (logistic/linear) with complex-sample procedures, including fixed country effects; for PIAAC skills, they use the plausible-values methodology requiring multiple imputation. Key results show that only 11% of teaching professionals have strong PS-in-TRE skills (Level 3) while 42% are weak (Level 1 or below), and age is the most consistent predictor: older teachers are more likely to have weak skills and greater need for ICT professional development. Associations between skills and attitudes/knowledge are generally weak (e.g., Pearson r=0.11 between measured skills and perceived job-relevant computer skills). Limitations include that skills and attitudes/knowledge come from different surveys and different participants, and that the TALIS items’ intercorrelations were too low to form reliable composite scales, so single-item analyses were used.
